547.title: Sent (Acts 13:1–3)
547.hook: while they fast and pray, Barnabas and Saul are set apart
547.howItsDone: Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on Lenten Fridays, many add small fasts of their own, and in ordination the bishop lays his hands on the one being ordained in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rhoda at the gate, so glad she left Peter knocking. Your line was she forgot to open.

Three verses. That's all Luke spends on the moment that starts the great journeys of Paul, the ones that carried the gospel across the Mediterranean. No vision on a road this time, no earthquake, no angel. Just a church in Antioch doing something ordinary: worshiping, and going without food.
screen: `THREE VERSES.` → `NO VISION THIS TIME.` → `AN ORDINARY CHURCH IN ANTIOCH.`

segments.voice: Luke bothers to list the names. In the church at Antioch there are prophets and teachers: Barnabas. Simeon, who was called Niger, a Latin nickname meaning dark or black. Lucius of Cyrene, from North Africa. Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, the same Herod who killed John the Baptist. And Saul, the former persecutor. A Cypriot, likely an African or two, a man raised in a royal court, and a converted enemy: that's the leadership. As they minister to the Lord and fast, the Holy Spirit speaks, paraphrased here: set apart for me Barnabas and Saul, for the work to which I have called them. The Greek word for set apart means to mark off, to separate for a purpose. Paul later begins his letter to the Romans calling himself separated for the gospel of God, the same root. And the church doesn't send them off at once. It fasts and prays again. Then they lay their hands on the two men, and send them away. The church let go of two of its five best teachers. Sending costs something. Catholics see a pattern here that the Church still follows: prayer and fasting before big decisions, and the laying on of hands to mark someone sent for a task, as in ordination today. And notice who speaks first in this story: not a committee, but the Spirit, heard by people who had made a little quiet by going without.

segments.voice: Picture one small thing you could go without, the phone at meals, the second coffee, the background noise in the car, and the gap it would leave; that gap is the kind of room the church in Antioch prayed in. In the quiet you have right now, ask what you might be set apart for: not a mission across the sea, maybe a person, a task, a conversation. If you pray, offer that small fast and simply listen.

548.title: The Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15)
548.hook: the first council decides Gentiles need not keep the whole Law
548.carry: it hath seemed good to the holy ghost
548.howItsDone: The Catholic Church counts its ecumenical councils from Nicaea to the Second Vatican Council, and looks to the gathering in Acts 15 as their model; bishops still meet in synods to discern together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Barnabas and Saul, sent out from Antioch while the church fasted. Your line was set apart.

A family over a will. A parish over a building. Some arguments can split a community in two, and for the first Christians, one came fast. Barnabas and Paul come back from their journey with news: Gentiles, non-Jews, are coming to believe. But some believers from Judea arrive in Antioch and teach that unless the Gentiles are circumcised and keep the Law of Moses, they cannot be saved. There was, the text says, no small dissension. So the church does something new: it goes to Jerusalem to decide together.
screen: `GENTILES ARE BELIEVING.` → `MUST THEY KEEP THE WHOLE LAW?` → `NO SMALL DISSENSION.`

segments.voice: It's worth being fair to both sides. The first believers were Jews who loved the Law. It was God's gift to Israel, and the question was a real one: if Gentiles join the people of Israel's Messiah, shouldn't they join Israel's covenant in full? So the apostles and elders gather, and there is much disputing. Peter stands and tells how God gave the Spirit to Gentiles at Cornelius's house, making no difference between them and us. Barnabas and Paul tell the signs God did among the nations, and the crowd falls silent to listen. Finally James, a leader of the Jerusalem church, speaks. He quotes the prophet Amos about the nations seeking the Lord, and proposes a way: don't trouble the Gentiles who are turning to God. Ask them only to keep away from food offered to idols, from blood and what is strangled, and from sexual immorality. Some readers see these as the things that let Jewish and Gentile believers share a table. Then they write a letter, and one sentence in it carries the whole method. In the Douay-Rheims: "For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us, to lay no further burden upon you than these necessary things." The Holy Ghost, and us. Not one man's ruling, and not a vote cut off from prayer, but a decision the whole gathering believed the Spirit had led. Catholics look to it as the pattern for the councils that followed, from Nicaea to the Second Vatican Council. And notice the order: they listened first, then decided.

segments.voice: Think of a decision you're facing that involves other people, at home, at work, in a group you belong to, and ask who hasn't been heard yet. If you pray, ask for the Holy Spirit's help before you decide.

549.title: Lydia (Acts 16:11–15)
549.hook: a businesswoman in purple cloth, the first convert in Europe, opens her home
549.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Lydia, and many parishes and Catholic homes practice hospitality through welcome ministries, shared meals and hosting prayer groups; in the early Church, believers met in homes like hers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the council in Jerusalem, listening before it decided. Your line was it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost.
screen: `IT HATH SEEMED GOOD TO THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Paul has just seen a vision in the night: a man of Macedonia, standing and begging, come over and help us. So Paul and his companions sail from Asia to the north of Greece, to Philippi, a Roman colony. They're expecting a man. On the Sabbath they walk out of the city gate to the riverside, where they think there's a place of prayer. And the people waiting there aren't men at all. It's a group of women. Paul sits down and starts talking with them.
screen: `COME OVER AND HELP US.` → `A RIVER OUTSIDE PHILIPPI.` → `NOT A MAN: A GROUP OF WOMEN.`

segments.voice: One of them is named Lydia, and Luke tells us three things about her in one breath. She's from Thyatira, a city back across the sea in Asia. She's a seller of purple, a costly dyed cloth, so she's a businesswoman, with a household and a house of her own. And she worships God: a Gentile who prays with the Jewish community. Then the line the whole story turns on, in the Douay-Rheims: "whose heart the Lord opened to attend to those things which were said by Paul." Notice who does the opening. Paul talks; the Lord opens; Lydia listens. She and her household are baptized, perhaps in that same river. Then she does something practical: if you judge me faithful to the Lord, she says, come and stay at my house. And Luke adds, she constrained us. She wouldn't take no for an answer. An opened heart becomes an opened door. Her house becomes the church of Philippi: after the jail scene coming tomorrow, Paul goes back to Lydia's house to see the brethren before leaving town. Years later, Paul writes to the Philippians, thanking them for their partnership from the first day. That church began on a riverbank, with a woman who sold purple cloth and opened her home.

segments.voice: Picture your front door: who has come through it lately, and who hasn't who might be glad to, a neighbor you only wave at, a friend who's been lonely, someone new at work or at church. It doesn't have to be dinner for twelve; coffee counts, a seat on the porch counts, so picture inviting that one person, simply and insistently, the way Lydia did. If you pray, ask that your heart be opened, like hers.

550.title: Midnight in the jail (Acts 16:25–34)
550.hook: Paul and Silas sing hymns in chains, and the jailer asks what must I do
550.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Liturgy of the Hours through the day and night, singing psalms and hymns, and the Church counts visiting the imprisoned among the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lydia, the seller of purple by the river. Your line was the lord opened her heart.

Still in Philippi, a few days later. A slave girl who tells fortunes earns her owners a lot of money. Paul, worn out by her following them around, casts the spirit out of her, and her owners watch their profits walk away. They drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates, and a crowd joins in. The two are stripped, beaten with rods, thrown into the inner prison, their feet fastened in the stocks. Bruised, bleeding, in the dark. A night like that could be spent in anger, or fear, or silence.
screen: `THE FORTUNE-TELLER'S OWNERS.` → `BEATEN WITH RODS.` → `FEET IN THE STOCKS.`

segments.voice: Here's what they do instead. In the Douay-Rheims: "And at midnight, Paul and Silas praying, praised God." The Greek says they were singing hymns. And a detail Luke didn't have to include: "they that were in prison, heard them." Suddenly there's an earthquake. The foundations shake, every door flies open, and everyone's chains come loose. The jailer wakes, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, since a jailer who lost his prisoners could expect to answer for it. And Paul cries out, in the Douay-Rheims: "Do thyself no harm, for we all are here." Nobody ran. The jailer calls for a light, rushes in trembling, falls down before them, and asks: "Masters, what must I do, that I may be saved?" Their answer is short: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your house. That same night, the man who locked their feet in the stocks washes their wounds. He and his whole household are baptized. He brings them into his house, sets food before them, and rejoices. Look at the shape of it: songs in the dark, an open door no one walks through, a jailer washing wounds. Years later, writing to this same church from another prison, Paul tells the Philippians to rejoice in the Lord always.

segments.voice: Think of the hardest place in your life right now, a worry, a room, a relationship, and pick a song you know by heart: a hymn if you have one, Amazing Grace, a Marian hymn, anything from Mass, or any song that has carried you before. Hum a line of it, or just hear it in your head, right there in the hard place; you don't have to feel cheerful, Paul and Silas had bleeding backs. If you pray, the song can be your prayer. And if the hard place is that you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

551.title: The unknown god (Acts 17:22–31)
551.hook: in Athens Paul says in him we live and move and are
551.howItsDone: Catholic teaching, especially the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate, speaks with respect of what is true and holy in other religions, and Catholics remember Dionysius the Areopagite as a saint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns, sung at midnight in the jail at Philippi by two beaten men. Your line was singing at midnight.

Athens. Even in Paul's day it was a kind of university town, famous for its past, full of temples, statues and people arguing in the marketplace. Paul is waiting there for his friends, walking the streets, and the city's statues stir him deeply. Philosophers hear him talking about Jesus and the resurrection and say, what is this babbler trying to say? So they bring him to the Areopagus, the hill where Athens heard new ideas, and ask him to explain. And Paul doesn't begin by attacking anyone.
screen: `ATHENS, A CITY OF ARGUMENTS.` → `WHAT IS THIS BABBLER SAYING?` → `UP TO THE AREOPAGUS.`

segments.voice: He begins with something he saw on his walk. Men of Athens, I see you are very religious. As I passed by, I found an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown God." What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you. That's his doorway: not their mistakes, but their own altar, their own honest admission that there was something they did not know. Then he describes God in words a Greek could follow. The God who made the world doesn't live in temples made by hands, and needs nothing from us, since he gives everyone life and breath. He made all nations from one, so that they would seek him, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him, though he is not far from any of us. Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "For in him we live, and move, and are." Paul even quotes their own poets: we are also his offspring. Those words come from the Greek poet Aratus, and Paul uses them to build a bridge. Only at the end does he speak of repentance, a day of judgment, and a man God raised from the dead. At the word resurrection, some laugh. Some say, we'll hear you again about this. And a few believe, including Dionysius, a member of the court, and a woman named Damaris. The Catholic Church draws on this speech when it teaches that other religions often reflect a ray of the truth, and that God is near to every person who seeks.

segments.voice: Think about the culture around you this week, a song stuck in your head, a show, a piece of art, a sports moment, and look for an altar in it, so to speak: some longing, some question, some reach toward something bigger that it never quite names. Paul looked at a city full of statues and found a doorway; let one doorway in yours come to mind. If you pray, remember that in him we live, and move, and are, even here.

552.title: Tentmakers (Acts 18)
552.hook: Priscilla and Aquila work with Paul and teach Apollos more perfectly
552.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saints Aquila and Priscilla, traditionally on July 8, and the Church teaches the dignity of ordinary work; many lay Catholics serve as catechists alongside their jobs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Areopagus in Athens, and the altar to the unknown God. Your line was in him we live.

Picture a workshop in Corinth, a busy port city. Leather and canvas, needles, awls, the smell of hides. Three people bent over their work, talking while they stitch. One of them is the Apostle Paul. It's easy to picture Paul only preaching to crowds or writing letters, and he did both. But much of his week, he was working with his hands to pay his own way. Luke tells us exactly what the job was: they were tentmakers.
screen: `A WORKSHOP IN CORINTH.` → `PAUL WITH A NEEDLE.` → `THEY WERE TENTMAKERS.`

segments.voice: The other two are a married couple, Aquila and Priscilla, Jews who had recently come from Rome, because the emperor Claudius had ordered Jews to leave the city. Paul stays with them, the text says, because they shared his trade. He works with them through the week, and on the Sabbath he speaks in the synagogue. The Greek word is skenopoioi, tent makers, though it may have meant leatherworkers more broadly. In a letter probably written from Corinth, Paul reminds the Thessalonians that he worked night and day so as not to be a burden to anyone. Now jump ahead. Priscilla and Aquila move with Paul to Ephesus, and a man named Apollos arrives from Alexandria: eloquent, mighty in the scriptures, on fire, teaching accurately about Jesus. But he knows only the baptism of John. So what do Priscilla and Aquila do? They don't correct him in front of everyone. In the Douay-Rheims, they "took him to them, and expounded to him the way of the Lord more diligently." The Greek means more exactly; older English Bibles put it as more perfectly, today's line. They take him aside, probably to their home, maybe their workshop, and fill in what he's missing. Then they send him on with letters of recommendation, and Apollos becomes a great help to the believers in Achaia. One more thing: more than once, Luke names Priscilla first. Many scholars think that means she was the better known of the two, maybe the leading teacher. Two tentmakers quietly shaped a preacher Paul later names in the same breath as himself and Peter. Catholics honor them as saints.
screen: `AQUILA AND PRISCILLA, FROM ROME.` · `PAUL WORKS WITH HIS HANDS.` · `APOLLOS, ELOQUENT, BUT MISSING SOMETHING.` · `THEY TOOK HIM ASIDE.` · then, large: `MORE PERFECTLY.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who is good at something, enthusiastic, maybe a little ahead of what they know: a new coworker, a younger relative, a friend who's just discovered something. Then think of who once did that for you, and if you pray, give thanks for them.

553.title: Eutychus (Acts 20:7–12)
553.hook: a young man falls asleep during Paul's long sermon and falls from a window
553.howItsDone: Catholics gather on Sunday, the first day of the week, for Mass, where the homily follows the Gospel and the Eucharist follows the homily; Sunday Mass is an obligation for Catholics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tentmakers, Priscilla and Aquila, taking Apollos aside. Your line was more perfectly.

A long homily, a late lecture, a meeting that runs past its hour: the Bible has a story for that. And the long speaker isn't some dull preacher. It's the Apostle Paul. The listener who nods off is a young man named Eutychus, sitting in an open window, three floors up. The room is crowded, the hour is late, and the lamps are burning. What happens next is both funny and serious, and it shows how one early church spent the first day of the week.
screen: `A LONG HOMILY.` → `THE SPEAKER IS PAUL.` → `A YOUNG MAN IN A WINDOW.`

segments.voice: It's Troas, a port on the coast of what is now Turkey. Luke sets the scene carefully, in the Douay-Rheims: "on the first day of the week, when we were assembled to break bread." We: the narrator was in the room. Sunday, the church gathered for the breaking of the bread. Paul is leaving the next day, so he has a lot to say, and he keeps talking until midnight. The upper room is crowded, with many lamps burning: warm, close and smoky. A young man named Eutychus is sitting in the window. And the text, with a straight face, says he sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on, fell from the third story, and was taken up dead. Everyone rushes down. Paul goes down too, throws himself on the young man, embraces him, and says: don't be troubled, his life is in him. Then the part that makes people laugh. Paul goes back upstairs, breaks the bread, eats, and keeps talking until daybreak. A man fell out the window, and even so, Paul went on. Meanwhile they bring the young man home alive, and the text says they were not a little comforted. His name, Eutychus, means fortunate. Luke may be smiling. But under the humor is an early picture of Christians gathering on the first day of the week to break bread, which Catholics read as the Eucharist, with a long sermon attached.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` · `PAUL TALKS UNTIL MIDNIGHT.` · `ASLEEP, AND OUT THE WINDOW.` · `HIS LIFE IS IN HIM.` · then, large: `AND PAUL WENT ON UNTIL DAYBREAK.`

segments.voice: Think of a speaker who tests your patience, a preacher, a teacher, a relative with long stories, a boss in meetings, and notice the impatience in your body. Picture them as someone who cares about what they're saying and maybe lacks the gift of brevity, and let a little of the irritation go; if you're the long talker sometimes, smile at that too. If you pray, pray for that person by name.
